title: A Non-Freaked Out Framework for Literacy Instruction Across the Content Areas, Common Core or Otherwise
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Stuart introduces version 2.0 of his 'non-freaked out' literacy framework and explains what he deliberately left out of it. He widens the audience to states whose college-and-career standards go by another name, arguing that the ideas matter more than the Common Core label. Invoking Jerry Graff's 'doctrine of simplicity', he defends a framework simple enough to grasp in an hour and complex enough to explore for a career. That is why choice reading, love of reading, research, and passion get no explicit place: the framework serves teachers in every subject, not only English. It puts argument and character at the center as themes to embed in all reading, writing, and speaking. Argument is taught as claim, evidence, and reasoning, always placed in relation to what others have said, after They Say / I Say. He then calls for quantifiable goals for how much students read, write, and speak in each course, for grade-level complexity with honest feedback, and for more attention to reading in order to gain knowledge. He grounds that last point in professors' complaints that students cannot learn from assigned textbooks.
points: Graff's 'doctrine of simplicity' - when several solutions reach the same end, pick the simplest - is Stuart's stated reason for leaving choice reading, research, and passion out of a cross-content framework.
He challenges teachers' sense of a 'right' to teach only what they love, asking whether they can become passionate about the challenge of teaching required curriculum well.

In his model of argument, claims made in isolation are not really arguments: students must accurately summarize what others have said before positioning their own view, which is how they come to answer 'so what?'.
Rather than spending days on laborious close reading, he follows Schmoker in setting quantifiable yearly targets for how many texts, paragraphs, debates, and discussions each course will require.
He singles out reading to gain knowledge as the standards' underemphasized skill, citing a nursing professor's report that students arrive unable to learn from assigned textbooks.
quotes: In putting forward this approach, I'm embracing what Jerry Graff called “the doctrine of simplicity” in a recent conversation we shared in the Chicago area. The basic premise of this idea is that if more than one solution to a problem can achieve the same end, then the simplest of the solutions is the best one.

In my 9th grade English classes, choice reading is a regular part of our routine, and I give my students time, space, encouragement, and one-on-one conferring to guide them toward developing a recreational reading habit. At the same time, I think ELA teachers are wise to avoid letting choice reading become the entire curriculum, as post-secondary settings require more than a love for choice reading (and professors I've spoken with seem to vigorously support that last statement).

But what if we can become passionate about just, you know, the challenge of teaching something we're not totally intrinsically thrilled by but that is a part of the curriculum regardless? What if we can become more alive at the thought of watching lights go on for our students rather than teaching that one text we've always wanted to teach or doing that one lab experiment we've always wanted to try?

I also like to pound into my students' heads several hundred times per class period the fact that arguments in isolation basically are not arguments — which means we need to read/listen to, accurately summarize, and then put forth our ideas in relation to what others have already said or written. If we do this, kids will begin answering the “so what?” question that educators around the nation crave to see in their students' work.

The same is true for writing and speaking. We need to provide kids with exemplar models of writing and speaking at a level appropriate to their age, and then we need to give them feedback that aims to be kind and honest, even when this means facing brutal gaps in their college and career readiness.

We've got to make sure 9th graders get ample chances to read texts that on-level 9th graders are reading. Interventions should be made for below-level readers, but every kid deserves to be taught how to read texts on pace for college and career-level complexity, even if he or she is drastically below grade-level. I disagree with those who say kids simply won't read what they can't — I think can't is a highly flexible term that depends on much more than a kid's SRI level.

Something I've not spent enough time exploring on Teaching the Core is the incredible importance of reading to gain knowledge. The Common Core mention the ability to build knowledge in the standards' introductory matter, but it's not emphasized nearly enough throughout the standards. Reading to know stuff is a big deal, both for college and careers.
